paras: The threatened lynching of eight Black youths at Camilla, Georgia, followed a hearing on Monday, January 16, 1888, at which eight youths described as 'negro boys' faced a charge of criminal assault on a young white woman. Four of them were sent to jail to await trial, and the threats of lynching that followed came to nothing.

According to the Savannah Morning News, the complainant was a young white woman from Colquitt county who had come to Camilla the previous Friday. The paper described her as 'half-witted' and 'of tarnished reputation', and it named neither her nor any of the accused.

At the Monday hearing, all eight youths answered the charge of criminal assault, and four were committed to jail to await trial. There were, in the paper's words, 'some threats of lynching them', but it did not say who made the threats or whether any crowd gathered. By the time the item was printed, 'all is now quiet', and no attack on the jail or the prisoners is reported.
No report of a trial, a grand jury action or the release of the other four youths appears in the coverage.

The episode survives in a single paragraph in the Savannah Morning News of January 20, 1888, printed in its 'Georgia and Florida' column of state news between items on a new Ocmulgee river steamer and the Young Men's Christian Association. The item had no headline or source of its own and treated the lynching threats in a closing clause, while its description of the woman cast doubt on her standing. No second newspaper account of the episode was found.

quotes: At Camilla eight negro boys had a hearing Monday on the charge of criminal assault upon a half-witted young white woman, of tarnished reputation, who came to town Friday from Colquitt county.
Four of the negroes were sent to jail to await trial. There were some threats of lynching them, but all is now quiet.
